concepts.name: High courts: origin, number, territorial jurisdiction, composition and appointment
concepts.description: How high courts began, how many there are and which areas they cover, how their strength is fixed and how judges are appointed (collegium and NJAC).
concepts.idea: A high court is created for each state (or jointly for several), has no fixed strength, and its judges are appointed by the President after consultation with the judiciary.
concepts.rule: High courts began in 1862 at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, with Allahabad added in 1866; the Seventh Amendment of 1956 let Parliament set up a common high court for two or more states, or states and a union territory. As per the standard count there were 25 high courts, only three of which have jurisdiction over more than one state; Delhi alone among the union territories has its own (since 1966), while Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh share one. Articles 214 to 231 deal with them. A high court consists of a chief justice and as many judges as the President thinks necessary, so its strength is not fixed by the Constitution. The chief justice is appointed by the President after consulting the Chief Justice of India and the governor; for other judges the chief justice of the high court is also consulted. The Second (1993) and Third (1998) Judges cases shaped the collegium, the 99th Amendment and NJAC Act of 2014 were struck down in 2015, and the collegium returned.
concepts.example: The Calcutta High Court, set up in 1862, today also covers the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

concepts.name: Qualifications, oath, salaries, tenure and removal of high court judges
concepts.description: Who can become a high court judge, the oath, pay, retirement, resignation and the impeachment procedure under the Judges Enquiry Act.
concepts.idea: A high court judge needs ten years at the bar or on the bench, serves to 62, and is removed in the same way and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge.
concepts.rule: A high court judge must be a citizen of India who has held judicial office in India for ten years or has been a high court advocate for ten years; no minimum age is prescribed and, unlike for the Supreme Court, a distinguished jurist cannot be appointed. The oath is taken before the governor or a person he appoints. Parliament fixes salaries, allowances, privileges, leave and pension, which cannot be varied to the judge's disadvantage except during a financial emergency. A judge holds office until 62 (raised from 60 by the 15th Amendment of 1963), may resign in writing to the President, and vacates office on appointment to the Supreme Court or transfer to another high court. Removal is by the President on an address of each House by special majority, in the same session, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity; the Judges Enquiry Act (1968) requires a motion signed by 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha members and a three-member committee.
concepts.example: A senior advocate with ten years of practice before a high court satisfies the qualification even if she has never been a judge.

concepts.name: Transfer of judges; acting chief justice; additional, acting and retired judges
concepts.description: Transfer of high court judges (Article 222) and the temporary arrangements of Articles 223, 224 and 224A.
concepts.idea: The President can transfer judges after consulting the Chief Justice of India, and can appoint acting, additional and (with consent) retired judges to deal with vacancies and arrears.
concepts.rule: The President may transfer a high court judge to another high court after consulting the Chief Justice of India; the judge receives a compensatory allowance fixed by Parliament. In 1977 the Supreme Court said transfers may be only an exceptional measure in public interest and not a punishment, and later that judicial review is necessary against arbitrary transfers, which, only the transferred judge can challenge. In the Third Judges case (1998) the Chief Justice of India was to consult the collegium of four senior-most Supreme Court judges and the chief justices of the two high courts concerned. The President may appoint an acting chief justice when the office is vacant or the chief justice is absent or unable to act, additional judges for up to two years to meet increased business or arrears, and acting judges for absent judges; additional and acting judges cannot serve beyond 62. A chief justice may, with the previous consent of the President and of the person, request a retired judge to sit temporarily; he enjoys the powers and privileges of a judge but is not otherwise deemed one.
concepts.example: A high court with a sudden backlog of pending appeals may be given additional judges for no more than two years.

concepts.name: Independence of the high court
concepts.description: The nine safeguards that protect high courts from executive and legislative pressure.
concepts.idea: High court judges are protected by consultative appointment, security of tenure, fixed service conditions, charged expenditure, immunity from discussion, post-retirement practice ban, contempt power, staff autonomy and entrenched jurisdiction.
concepts.rule: Nine safeguards protect the independence of high courts. Judges are appointed by the President (in effect the cabinet) in consultation with the judiciary, which curtails executive discretion. They enjoy security of tenure: they can be removed only as the Constitution provides and do not hold office during the pleasure of the President. Salaries, allowances, privileges, leave and pension are fixed by Parliament and cannot be varied to their disadvantage except in a financial emergency. Judges' salaries and allowances, the staff's salaries, allowances and pensions and the court's administrative expenses are charged on the state's Consolidated Fund and are non-votable but can be discussed, while a judge's pension is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Their conduct cannot be discussed in Parliament or a state legislature except during an impeachment motion; retired permanent judges cannot plead before any court or authority except the Supreme Court and other high courts; the court can punish for contempt; the chief justice appoints the staff; and jurisdiction specified in the Constitution cannot be curtailed by Parliament or the state legislature.

concepts.name: Jurisdiction of the high court: original, writ and appellate
concepts.description: Sources of high court jurisdiction, its original jurisdiction, writ jurisdiction under Article 226 (compared with Article 32) and civil and criminal appeals.
concepts.idea: A high court is primarily a court of appeal, but it also hears some cases first, and its writ power under Article 226 is wider than the Supreme Court's.
concepts.rule: The Constitution keeps a high court's jurisdiction and powers the same as immediately before its commencement, adding revenue matters, writs and superintendence. Original jurisdiction covers election disputes of legislators, revenue matters, fundamental rights and cases transferred from subordinate courts involving interpretation of the Constitution; Calcutta, Bombay, Madras and Delhi also have original civil jurisdiction in cases of higher value, while the original criminal jurisdiction of the first three was abolished by the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973. Article 226 lets a high court issue writs for fundamental rights and for any other purpose, even outside its territory if the cause of action arises within it (15th Amendment, 1963); this is concurrent with Article 32 but wider, and the Chandra Kumar case (1997) made it part of the basic structure. Appellate jurisdiction is wider than original: first appeals on law and fact, second appeals on law only, intra-court appeals to a division bench, appeals from tribunals, and in criminal matters appeals where the sentence exceeds seven years, with confirmation of death sentences.
concepts.example: A citizen whose fundamental right is violated by a state authority may move the high court under Article 226 instead of going straight to the Supreme Court.

concepts.name: Supervisory jurisdiction, control over subordinate courts, court of record and judicial review
concepts.description: Superintendence over courts and tribunals, administrative control of subordinate courts, the high court as a court of record and its power of judicial review.
concepts.idea: A high court supervises all courts and tribunals in its territory (except military ones), controls the subordinate judiciary, records its decisions as precedent, and can strike down unconstitutional laws.
concepts.rule: A high court has the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals in its territory except military courts or tribunals: it can call for returns, make general rules, prescribe forms and settle fees. The power is broad, extending to courts whether or not subject to its appeals, covering administrative and judicial superintendence, revisional and suo motu, but it is extraordinary and used sparingly. The governor consults the high court on appointment, posting and promotion of district judges; the court handles posting, promotion, leave, transfer and discipline of other judicial service members, can withdraw a case involving a substantial constitutional question, and its law binds subordinate courts. As a court of record it keeps its proceedings as precedent and punishes contempt of itself and, under the Contempt of Courts Act 1971, of subordinate courts; it can review its own judgements. Judicial review under Articles 13 and 226 rests on three grounds; the 42nd Amendment curtailed it and the 43rd Amendment restored it.
concepts.example: A high court may call for the records of a tribunal in a district and quash an order that shows a gross violation of natural justice.
